list.listitem: Congenital hydrocephalus is rare, and occurs in less than 0.6 per 1000 live births. Over 40% of infants have other associated malformations, most commonly facial clefts, cardiac defects, or renal malformations. C
Clinical signs may be subtle in infants and a thorough neurological examination is necessary when an infant has increasing head circumference percentiles. C
Evaluation should include a family history, tests for prenatal infections, DNA analysis, and cytogenetic studies when indicated. C
Prenatal surgery for myelomeningocele in appropriately selected patients reduces the likelihood of postnatal development of shunt dependent hydrocephalus. B
Ventricloperitoneal (VP) shunt and endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) have similar outcomes.C
Prognosis is poor: 25% of patients die within the first week after birth; mortality is 40% by 1 year of age. B

background.definition: Congenital hydrocephalus is part of a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by abnormalities in the flow or resorption of cerebrospinal fluid, resulting in increased pressure. The diagnosis excludes the presence of neural tube defects, intraventricular hemorrhage, and intracranial tumors.

list.listitem: 46 per 100,000 live births (CI, 3.75-5.74) in Europe.
A systematic review found an incidence of 81/100,000 live births over an 11 year period. The incidence was lower in high income countries.
Noncerebral major malformations are present in 44%, most frequently limb defects, congenital heart disease, facial clefts, and renal malformations.
The recurrence rate for autosomal recessive forms is estimated to be 1% to 4%.

About 50% of patients have isolated hydrocephalus (absence of associated anomalies except the one producing the hydrocephalus). About half of patients with isolated hydrocephalus have one of three etiologies: Chiari II malformation, aqueductal stenosis, or Dandy-Walker malformation.
Another 45% of patients have recognized syndromes or multiple malformations.
About 5% have an X-linked recessive form.

A retrospective cohort study using a Danish birth registry identified the following risk factors for congenital hydrocephalus: first trimester exposure to maternal use of antidepressants (RR 2.5, 95% CI 1.5-4.3), male gender, multiple pregnancy, and maternal diabetes.
Obstruction to the flow of CSF by aqueductal stenosis leads to enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles.
In malformations of the posterior fossa such as Dandy-Walker syndrome, communication to the subarachnoid space from the fourth ventricle is obstructed, leading to enlargement of all ventricles.
CSF resorption may be disturbed in some chromosomal abnormalities.
Prenatal ultrasound done for routine screening or for other indications may not detect hydrocephalus if done before 20 weeks' gestation. C

A systematic review and guideline concluded that prenatal surgery for myelomeningocele in appropriately selected patients reduces the likelihood of postnatal development of shunt dependent hydrocephalus. B
Infants may present with a history of irritability, lethargy, poor feeding, or vomiting; on exam infants will have a bulging, wide fontanelle, a broad forehead, and dilated scalp veins. C
Perform head ultrasound to confirm enlarged ventricles; MRI may be needed to accurately define the extent of hydrocephalus and presence of brain malformations. C
Test to exclude other causes of hydrocephalus such as infection. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Normal intelligence, normal to mild motor delay, increased parental head circumference
Other signs consistent with chronic anemia, osteogenesis imperfecta, epiphyseal dysplasias
Parietal bossing, presence of subdural collections on imaging
Signs specific to lysosomal disorders, aminoacidurias, leukodystrophies

list.listitem: Infants may present with a history of irritability, lethargy, poor feeding, or vomiting. Occasionally, stridor and hoarse cry may be the presenting symptom.
On physical examination, infants will have a bulging, wide fontanelle, a broad forehead, and dilated scalp veins. Sutures may be split.

Neurological examination may reveal long tract signs present initially as brisk lower extremity reflexes, and proceed to clonus. Abducens nerve palsy may be present. "Setting-sun sign" (downward deviation of the eyes) is a late sign.

Neurocutaneous markers suggest diagnoses other than congenital hydrocephalus. Cafe-au-lait macules and axillary or inguinal freckling suggest neurofibromatosis, while tufts of hair, angioma or lipoma on the spine suggest spinal dysraphism.
Ophthalmologic examination: Look for chorioretinitis (toxoplasmosis); papilledema may be present after sutural closure (9-18 months of age).

After treatment by shunting, monitor for signs of shunt malfunction. In order of likelihood these include bulging fontanel in infants, fluid collection along the shunt, reduced consciousness or irritability, headache, nausea or vomiting, and bradycardia with or without hypertension. Loss of upward gaze is highly significant, but rare.

Also monitor for shunt infection during intercurrent illnesses; the presence of fever and proximity to initial shunt operation (<6 months) are highly predictive of shunt infection. Other signs that are rare but increase the likelihood of shunt infection are purulent drainage, skin erosion, meningismus, erythema, peritonitis, abdominal pain, and CSF leakage.
Prenatal ultrasound: More than a third of patients are detected after 24 weeks' gestation.

When clinically suspected, order postnatal head ultrasound and head MRI to assess diameter of lateral ventricle (LV). Borderline ventriculomegaly = 10-12 mm and mild = 12-15 mm. Borderline ventriculomegaly may be a normal finding in large fetuses close to term and in male fetuses (who are in general larger than females).
Order serological tests for prenatal infections: toxoplasmosis, cytomegalovirus (CMV), rubella, mumps, varicella.
Order genetic evaluation for recognizable syndrome or chromosomal disorder (karyotype and cytogenetics).
In hydrocephalic adults with suspected shunt malfunction, radionuclide shuntography is only moderately accurate (LR+ 2, LR- 0.3).
Children with ventricular shunts are often subjected to frequent CT scans, which usually do not result in a change in management. Thoughtful and not routine ordering of imaging is important.
Polyhydramnios or oligohydramnios is present in ~20% of pregnancies, and may be the only prenatal sign of the disorder at 20 weeks.
Prenatal diagnosis is based on visualization of dilated ventricles on ultrasound. Postnatally, the diagnosis is suspected by poor infant feeding, lethargy, vomiting, or eye deviation.

Criteria for diagnosis are based on the presence of increased head circumference (head circumference at birth >2 SD for gestational age and birth length, or an increase in head circumference to >2 SD for age and mean height in the first year of life) and increased intracranial fluid (presence of increased intraventricular fluid volume as shown by an increased LV/hemisphere ratio (LV/H) by ultrasound and MRI).
Further evaluation should include a family history, tests for prenatal infections, DNA analysis, and cytogenetic studies when indicated.
See .
Treatment is neurosurgical with placement of shunt. C
Optimize nutrition and development with physical, occupational, and speech therapy. C

A Cochrane review concluded that systemic antibiotics (OR 0.52) and antibiotic impregnated catheters (OR 0.21) reduce the rate of shunt infection in the first 24 hours. However, there is no evidence that they reduce all-cause mortality or provide longer-term benefits.

A randomized trial studied 60 patients with congenital hydrocephalus underoing VP shunt insertion whoh all received conventional perioperative antibiotics. One group received vancomycin and gentamicin injection in the reservoir and around the peritoneal catheter either once or twice, while the control group received only standard perioperative antibiotic. There were 20 patients in each grouop, and the groups receiving vancomycin and gentamicin had only one shunt infection, compared with 6 in the control group.

A meta-analysis of 9 studies compared topical, intraventricular or both antibiotics with placebo and found lower rates of shunt infection with antibiotics (2.2% vs 5.2%, p < 0.05, NNT = 33). Most studies used vancomycin, vancomycin+gentamicin, or bacitracin.

A 2014 guideline concluded, based on a systematic review of 14 studies, that ventricloperitoneal (VP) shunt and endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) had equivalent outcomes. The guideline also recommended preoperative antibiotics to prevent shunt infection (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.38-0.81 based on a meta-analysis).

A systematic review (2025) identified 6 case reports and 6 case series of patients undergoing surgical treatment for fetal hydrocephalus. While VP shunting is superior for gait improvement, LP shunting may offer better cognitive preservation.
Surgical shunt placement to decompress the cerebral ventricles is the standard therapy, although randomized trials do not exist in the literature.

Ventriculoperitoneal shunts have a 35% to 40% failure rate in the first year of life; attrition continues, but at a much lower rate subsequently. Failure may be due to mechanical obstruction, excessive CSF drainage, fracture, migration, or infection. The most common causes in infants younger than 2 years are infection and shunt obstruction.

Pedictors of VP shunt failure in children include revision rather than initial placement. It was more common in those with a history of seizures (OR 1.4, 95% CI 1.0-3.3) or cardiac risk factors (OR 1.3, 95% CI 1.0-1.7), but less common in those with a history of neuromuscular disease (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.41-0.90).

A review of 1570 VP shunt procedures found that an infection occurred in 4.0%, with a mean of 19 days between procedure and infection. Risk factors for VP shunt infection include history of 2 or more previous revisions (OR 4.8) and age less than 5 years (OR 4.5), while neoplastic cause of hydrocephalus was protective.

A randomized trial compared gradual reduction of the opening pressure to 7 cm H2O with a fixed pressure setting of 13 cm H2O in 68 patients with idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus. While there was no difference in complication rates between groups, clinical improvement was better in the group with a gradually lowered opening pressure.

A systematic review of 8 retrospective cohort studies with 590 children compared distal laparoscopic placement in 39% with open surgical placement in 51%. The rates of distal revision were similar (3.75% vs. 4.3%, p = 0.74) as were shunt infection rates (laparoscopic 5.6% vs. open 7.5%, p= 0.97). Surgery time was shorter in the laparoscopic group (49 vs. 64 minutes, p= 0.03).
Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV)
A 2014 guideline concluded, based on a systematic review of 14 studies, that ventricloperitoneal (VP) shunt and endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) had equivalent outcomes.

A randomized trial in Uganda compared ETV with VP shunt placement. At 12 months, cognitive scores were similar as were motor or language scores. This study found better outcomes for ETV after 3 months of age compared with before 3 months of age.

A systematic review of 10 observational studies (6 retrospective) concluded that there was no difference between ETV and VP shunt with regards to symptom improvement, hematoma or mortality but there was a lower complication rate and less need for repeat surgery. However, selection bias, confounding, and other factors limit the ability to draw firm conclusions from these data.

A systematic review of case series and small observational studies found that patients treated with flexible as opposed to rigid neuroendoscopy for ETV had lower expected success pre-operatively but ultimately had similar outcomes. Selection bias is likely a factor in these studies.
Early physical therapy, occupational therapy, and speech therapy may optimize development.
Gene therapy is currently being explored to correct the defect in the choroid plexus that leads to build-up fluid.

Multidisciplinary approach is essential. This includes a developmental pediatrician; neurologist; neurosurgeon; ancillary services such as physical, occupational and speech therapy; gastroenterologist and nutritionist if swallowing dysfunction and failure to thrive is present; and geneticist if chromosomal or syndromic etiology is suspected.
Primary care physicians need to monitor for evidence of shunt block (signs of raised intracranial pressure (ICP)) and shunt infection during intercurrent illnesses.

A 2014 guideline concluded based on systematic reviews that in addition to antibiotics, either partial or complete shunt removal is an option. The selection of a specific approach is at the discretion of the surgeon.

Use of intrathecal antibiotics in addition to systemic antibiotics is not supported by evidence in cases where the shunt can't be removed or must be removed and replaced immediately during ongoing infection.

Following shunt malfunction, endoscopic third ventriculostomy instead of shunt revision has rates of shunt malfunction at 3, 6 and 12 months of 66%, 63% and 53% based on 16 studies with 584 patients. New neurologic deficits occurred in 1.6%.

Shunt migration is one complication of ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement. The most commonn site of migration was the scrotum (30%) followed by anus, bowel, chest wall, and intracranial or subgaleal migration.
Fetal and neonatal death occur more frequently in those with associated malformations. B

A systematic review of registries identified 13,112 cases of congenital hydrocephalus out of over 19 million total births. Early neonatal case fatality rate was 5.9 per 100 liveborn infants (95% CI 5.4 - 6.8). B
More than half of survivors have developmental and neurological deficits. B
Children with no associated abnormalities and a normal karyotype have a better developmental prognosis. B

cell.label: HISTORY: Infant with poor feeding, lethargy, vomiting, eye deviation

Physical examination (PE): look for bulging fontanel, split sutures, rapid increase in head circumference, downward gaze deviation or abducens palsy, and long tract signs (brisk deep tendon reflexes or clonus)
Obtain an emergency head ultrasound, and possibly MRI. Treatment based on findings

History: slow motor development. Ask about maternal history (infections during pregnancy, possible exposure to teratogens including alcohol), family history (hydrocephalus, intellectual disability, spastic paraplegia), and consanguinity (focusing on males related through females).

PE: Head circumference: rapid rise or >2 SD for age and length ASSESS FOR • Linear growth pattern • Dysmorphic features, limb defects • Bulging fontanel, split sutures, downward gaze deviation or abducens palsy • Long tract signs: brisk deep tendon reflexes or clonus • Neurocutaneous markers (for spinal dysraphism) • Ophthalmologic examination (for toxoplasmosis or CMV)

• Obtain a head ultrasound to assess ventriculomegaly • Evaluate for causes of chronic anemia • Serological tests to look for infectious etiology: toxoplasmosis, CMV, rubella, mumps, varicella • DNA and cytogenetic studies when indicated • Neurosurgical referral • Genetics evaluation
Measure parental head circumference for size >2 SD above the adult mean
Consider familial megalencephaly. Monitor motor development
